title: Caching (cache-aside / write-through / write-back, eviction, Redis/Memcached, CDN, invalidation)
relevance: High — almost every HLD "design X" round; FAANG and Indian product cos expect you to place a cache, pick a write strategy, name eviction + invalidation, and discuss stampede / stale-read tradeoffs when the DB or origin is the bottleneck.
company_notes: Campus/intern HLD treats Redis + CDN as table stakes in URL shortener, feed, e-commerce, chat, TikTok/YouTube; mid-level (1–4 YOE) probes stampedes, hot keys, Redis vs Memcached, write-back risk, and CDN purge vs versioned assets at Amazon, Meta, Google, Uber, Atlassian, Flipkart. Near-universal HLD building block; deep consistency follow-ups common; full "design Memcached" rarer outside infra-heavy loops.

phases.goal: Establish why you cache, where layers sit, and what is worth caching.

must_hit.point: Cache stores a hot subset in fast memory to cut latency and shield the DB/origin; hit ratio is the goal metric and a miss costs a full DB/origin round-trip (plus possible stampede).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states latency/DB protection as the purpose and names hit ratio vs miss cost.

must_hit.point: Placement stack is browser/client → CDN → reverse proxy → app local (in-process) → distributed cache (Redis/Memcached) → DB buffer pool.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks the layers end-to-end rather than only naming Redis.

must_hit.point: Prefer caching read-heavy, slowly changing, expensive-to-compute data — do not cache everything.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says what not to cache and ties choice to read/write and change rate.

probes: Why introduce a cache in a design, and where would you place it between the client and the database?

hints.1: Think about what hurts when the DB or origin is the bottleneck.
hints.2: Name the layers from browser/CDN down to Redis and the DB buffer pool.
hints.3: Hot subset in fast memory → higher hit ratio; miss = full origin round-trip; cache read-heavy, slowly changing, expensive data.

phases.goal: Show how read/write patterns, invalidation, and eviction actually work.

must_hit.point: Cache-aside (lazy loading): app checks cache → miss → read DB → populate cache; flexible, app owns consistency, first request after miss/expiry is slow — default interview pattern.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes the miss path and that the app owns consistency.

must_hit.point: Write-through writes cache and DB synchronously (stronger freshness / read-your-writes, slower writes); write-back writes cache first and flushes DB async (fast writes, data loss if cache dies before flush).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts sync dual-write vs async flush and names the crash risk for write-back.

must_hit.point: On DB update, prefer delete-after-DB-write of the cache key (idempotent) so the next read refills; TTL is a backstop, not a substitute for explicit invalidation when freshness matters.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate sketches write DB → DEL key → next GET refill and treats TTL as safety net.

must_hit.point: When memory is full, eviction choices include LRU (default interview answer), LFU (skewed hot sets), TTL, and random; Redis pairs maxmemory with a policy such as allkeys-lru for pure caches.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names LRU/LFU/TTL and mentions Redis maxmemory + policy.

probes: Walk me through cache-aside on a miss, then how you'd invalidate after a DB update — and when would you use write-through or write-back instead?

hints.1: Start with who checks the cache on read, then what happens on write.
hints.2: Separate read path (aside vs read-through) from write path (through vs back) and from delete-vs-TTL.
hints.3: Aside: miss→DB→populate; invalidate with DB-first then DEL; write-through = sync cache+DB; write-back = async flush with loss risk; LRU + maxmemory for eviction.

phases.goal: Force explicit choices among write strategies, Redis vs Memcached, and CDN vs app cache.

must_hit.point: Write-through favors freshness and read-your-writes but slows writes and can pollute the cache with rarely-read keys; write-back favors write speed but risks data loss and fits counters/analytics, not money/passwords.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate maps freshness vs durability to the two write strategies with concrete unfit examples.

must_hit.point: Memcached is a simple multi-threaded string/object cache without rich types/persistence; Redis adds structures (hashes, sets, sorted sets), optional persistence, replication/cluster, pub/sub, scripting — default unless you only need dumb GET/SET at extreme throughput.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate picks Redis for structures/HA needs and Memcached for simple high-throughput GET/SET.

must_hit.point: CDN is an edge layer for static (and some dynamic) bytes near users with origin pull on miss and purge on deploy; Redis is objects near services — complementary layers, not substitutes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate assigns media to CDN and session/feed metadata/counters to Redis.

probes: Product catalog vs wallet balance vs view counters — which write strategy, and why Redis over Memcached? Where does a CDN fit vs the app cache?

hints.1: Ask what "wrong" means: stale, lost write, or slow write.
hints.2: Map catalog→aside+TTL, wallet→write-through, counters→write-back; then Redis features vs Memcached simplicity; CDN for media.
hints.3: Aside+TTL for minutes-old catalog; write-through for read-your-writes balance; write-back only if loss OK; Redis for structures/replication; CDN for images/video, Redis for feed/session/counters.

phases.goal: Apply patterns to stampede, invalidation races, outages, and a multi-layer design.

must_hit.point: Stampede/thundering herd: hot key expiry triggers many DB loads; mitigations include single-flight/lock (SETNX), probabilistic early refresh, jittered TTLs, and serving stale while one request refills.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the viral-key expiry failure and at least two mitigations from the list.

must_hit.point: Cache penetration (repeated misses for missing keys) is mitigated by caching negative/null with short TTL; hot keys hammer one shard; whole-cache outage sends every request to DB — need degrade path, circuit breaker, or small local fallback.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes penetration, hot key, and full outage with a degrade strategy.

must_hit.point: Delete-before-DB-write can reintroduce stale data; updating cache before DB commit can leave phantom values on crash — classic fix is DB-first then invalidate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains the race/phantom and lands on DB-first + invalidate.

probes: A celebrity profile TTL hits zero at peak QPS — what fails, and how do you protect the DB? If Redis is down, how do you avoid melting Postgres?

hints.1: Picture every instance missing at once on the same key.
hints.2: Cover stampede mitigations, then outage: fail-open with shedding vs local last-known vs fail-closed.
hints.3: Single-flight/SETNX, jittered TTL, serve-stale-while-revalidate; on Redis down use shedding/circuit breaker/local fallback so Postgres is not overwhelmed.

tradeoffs.topic: cache-aside + TTL vs write-through vs write-back
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Catalog (read-heavy, minutes-old OK) → cache-aside+TTL; wallet balance (read-your-writes) → write-through; view counters (write-heavy, loss OK) → write-back. Wrong pick: aside leaves balance stale, write-through slows counter writes and pollutes cache, write-back risks losing money/password updates on cache crash.

Freshness-critical updates: write DB then DEL key so next GET refills; TTL is a backstop. TTL-only is acceptable when minutes-old data is fine or updates bypass the app (batch jobs) and you lack CDC/events. Delete-before-DB-write can reintroduce stale data; set-new-value races are worse than idempotent delete.

Choose Redis for structures (sessions, rate limits, leaderboards), persistence, replication/cluster, pub/sub. Memcached wins for simple multi-threaded GET/SET at extreme throughput with no rich types or persistence needs.

CDN: geo edge for images/video segments, origin pull on miss, purge/versioned URLs on replace. Redis: feed fanout metadata, sessions, counters near services. Different layers — bytes near users vs objects near app.

Write-through: synchronous cache+DB → stronger freshness, slower writes, possible rarely-read pollution. Write-back: fast writes, async DB flush, data loss if cache dies before flush — not for durable critical data.

gotchas.trap: Treating cache invalidation as solved once you have a cache
gotchas.correction: Races between fill and invalidate, multi-writer apps, and updates that bypass the app (batch jobs) still need TTL and/or CDC/event invalidation.

gotchas.trap: Caching mutable, user-specific, or security-sensitive data without short TTL / auth scoping
gotchas.correction: Wrong user can see wrong data — scope keys to auth and keep TTLs short for sensitive mutable data.

gotchas.trap: Drawing Redis without key design, TTL, or eviction policy
gotchas.correction: Interviewers probe all three: how keys are named, when they expire, and what happens at maxmemory (e.g. allkeys-lru).

gotchas.trap: Updating the cache before the DB commits
gotchas.correction: Crash leaves phantom cache values; write DB first, then invalidate (delete) the key.

gotchas.trap: Ignoring stampede on the hottest keys because overall hit ratio looks fine
gotchas.correction: One viral key expiry can still overload the DB; add single-flight, jitter, or serve-stale-while-revalidate.

gotchas.trap: Assuming CDN purge is instant everywhere
gotchas.correction: Edges can lag; versioned URLs (e.g. asset.v3.js) often beat emergency purge.

gotchas.trap: Assuming write-back is always faster and fine
gotchas.correction: Interviewer will ask about crash before flush — data loss makes it unfit for money/passwords.
